Dermatology · published research

Sensitive skin

In a 30-person randomized trial, both LED regimens improved sensitive-skin symptom scores versus emollient control. Yellow light also improved erythema, water loss through the skin, and sting-test outcomes, while earlier uncontrolled studies reported symptom improvement.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In a 30-person randomized trial, both LED regimens improved sensitive-skin symptom scores versus emollient control. Yellow light also improved erythema, water loss through the skin, and sting-test outcomes, while earlier uncontrolled studies reported symptom improvement.

Summary of the Evidence

Three exact-category publications include one prospective randomized trial with 30 participants, one uncontrolled 30-person pilot, and one uncontrolled 28-person clinical study that also included a keratinocyte experiment. No overlap between the clinical groups is reported. The randomized study is the only controlled clinical comparison in this small evidence base.

Human and clinical evidence

In the 2026 trial, participants were assigned to emollient control, 590-nm LED, or combined 590/630-nm LED. Both light groups had greater improvement in sensitive-skin symptom scores than control. The yellow-light group also had lower erythema and melanin indices, reduced transepidermal water loss, and better lactic-acid sting-test results. The combined yellow-and-red group had lower sting scores than control. No adverse events were reported in the trial (He et al. 2026).

An earlier single-arm pilot of 30 people reported that symptom scores fell after treatment and remained lower at a two-month check. With no control group, these changes cannot separate a light effect from expectation, changes in skin care, or natural fluctuation. A 28-person study of polarized light also reported lower erythema and symptom measures, but used a broad spectrum and repeated treatment, so it is not the same protocol as narrow-band LED therapy.

Animal evidence

No animal study directly addressing sensitive skin was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

The 28-person report included an experiment with sodium-lauryl-sulfate-irritated keratinocytes. Polarized-light exposure reduced release of vascular endothelial growth factor in the cell model. This is a laboratory outcome from the same publication as the uncontrolled clinical series, not a separate patient cohort.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The randomized trial used 590-nm yellow visible light at 10 mW/cm² for 11 minutes three times weekly, or combined 590-nm yellow and 630-nm red visible light at 30 mW/cm² for 10 minutes three times weekly. Treatment lasted eight weeks. The earlier polarized-light protocol covered a much broader visible and infrared range. No study compares these approaches directly or establishes whether the effects continue after treatment ends.

Interpretation

The randomized comparison found improvements in symptoms and several objective or provocation measures, which supports short-term benefit for the tested LED protocols. Earlier uncontrolled results point in the same direction. Replication is needed to determine the typical effect size and durability, but the current controlled finding is more informative than case-level observations alone.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for short-term symptom improvement with 590-nm or 590/630-nm LED treatment
Publications and records3 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

A small randomized trial found better symptom scores than emollient control and improvements in several measured skin-barrier or sting-test outcomes. Two earlier uncontrolled reports point in a similar direction, including one laboratory component. The total sample remains small, so a larger independently replicated trial with follow-up after treatment would help establish how long the changes last.
